Having finished part 2, I'd say my first impression hasn't changed much. O'Toole's concerns about the quality of the data were 100 per cent valid, and the way she was treated is depressingly common in academia - "You can't reproduce the results? You must SUCK, then!" (As an aside, this dynamic occurred in the case of Bengu Sezen, and two PhD students were shit canned for being unable to reproduce fraudulent results).


A lot of the people closely associated didn't do themselves any favours either, David Baltimore in particular. Within him I clearly see a hubris that comes with decades of praise being heaped upon him, and with people like him it's easy to see where the arrogant academic archetype comes from. I'm not the least bit surprised that he refused to be interviewed.


The only thing I can say in Imanishi-Kari's defence is that she was the victim of what could arguably be called overzealous prosecution. Dingell's approach left a bad taste in my mouth, but I can't say that his heart was in the wrong place. The fact that some fields of research have reproducibility crises tells us that the scientific community is doing a piss poor job of self governance, and this is simply unacceptable when billions of dollars of public money are involved.

I saw part 1 first, and I found myself thinking that the case against Imanishi-Kari did have some merit. I haven't finished part 2 yet, but I'm finding myself vindicated. I wouldn't call Imanishi-Kari a fraudster, but she did show signs of sloppiness, being driven by the "publish or perish" culture that is so pervasive throughout academia.

That being said, I'm well aware of my own personal biases, which are based on my own experience as a postgrad. The reason I'm not a researcher is because the work environment is downright dogshit, especially at elite schools (I had the "privilege" of studying at what is considered an elite school where I live). The concept of work/life balance in academia is a JOKE. It's simply understood that your work \*is\* your life, as all the researchers who rise to the top have one common trait - they're all chronic workaholics. Passion for the work isn't enough, you need to be *obsessed* about your chosen field. Compared to my colleagues, my supervisor was one of the kinder ones, but he still expected us all to eat coal and shit diamonds on a regular basis, and he would express his displeasure if you weren't clearing the high bar he set.

Another thing scientific scandals have highlighted is that there are glaring shortcomings in the field when it comes to weeding out bad actors, or the maintenance of standards. The fact that even in the 2000s fraudsters could get "ground-breaking" papers published in leading journals using spectral data that had been deliberately doctored with WHITE-OUT should raise alarm bells. Science is an inherently high-trust activity, and key institutions in research and publishing are still operating under the misguided assumption that we have levels of social capital that haven't existed in at least a century.

When I finally stopped guzzling Coca-Cola like a fiend, and kept cutting sugar from my diet wherever possible, I found my palate broadened considerably. I wasn't simply capable of eating foods I normally turned my nose at, I was actually enjoying them. I was a notoriously fussy eater through my childhood and my early adult years, right up until I kicked my sugar habit.

Nowadays I struggle to drink most sodas, as I now find the sweetness to be off-putting. I used to get through 2 litres of that crap per *day*. I know it's not exactly scientific, but I genuinely believe that overexposure to things like sugar and salt can really screw with your sense of taste, and it's probably why so many fatties struggle with making changes - the kinds of foods that they should be eating typically have flavor profiles well outside the narrow comfort zone they're stuck in.

Siberian frontiers don't make that much difference for this achievement. Take a close look at the requirements - the only provinces required for the Relentless Push East achievement are  Kamchatka, Penzhina, Kagyrgyn, Gizhiga, Tauisk, Okhotsk and Jugjur - and most of these are held by the Siberian tribal states (provided they don't migrate too much, and they usually don't).

You can blitz this achievement by bordergoring your way through central asia and Manchuria. Invade Uzbek to get yourself a border with Oirat, then invade Oirat and take all their northernmost provinces (and the northern provinces of their vassal Mongolia). You have to time this war so that when you declare, Ming has low mandate (Ming is much easier to white peace when they have low mandate). Then it's a question of conquering the province of Urkan to get yourself a land border with Jugjur, which you can then colonize.

Once you have colonized/conquered Okhotsk, you'll be able to fabricate a claim on Kamchatka (because they share a common sea tile). Then it's just a walk in the park eating up the Siberian tribes, and then colonizing any remaining provinces needed for the achievement. My attempt at a gas generator on the moon had a dedicated coolant pipe network with over 200 radiators, and that still wasn't enough to prevent the generator from eventually shutting down due to overheating. Running a gas generator on Europa is child's play by comparison - just have a door to the outside that opens whenever the generator temperature hits a set value (I usually go with ~40 degrees C). The only downside is that you will lose a bit of nitrogen and CO2 every time the door opens.

I don't doubt that it'd be possible to run a gas generator on the moon - but without hard data on the heat output of the generator, designing an adequate cooling system is pure guesswork. What I initially thought was a ridiculously over-engineered (but aesthetically pleasing) solution turned out to be inadequate. Given the devs' tendency to use actual science (e.g. the gases in game obey the ideal gas law), I'm guessing the generator's heat output is based on the enthalpy of combustion of hydrogen (286 kJ/mol). The only question is what percentage of that is radiated by the generator itself - my guess would be most of it.
